analysis.title: Dip buying lifts US stocks after tech slide (UBS House View - CIO Alert)
key_insights: US stocks rose sharply Monday 11/9 as investors returned to tech and growth after last week's sell-off. S&P 500 closed +2.4%, Nasdaq +2.7%.

Semiconductors led: Philadelphia Semiconductor Index +6.9%, while NVIDIA fell 4.3% after an internal investigation into its CEO Jensen Huang began. Most S&P 500 sectors advanced, with consumer discretionary and communication services among the strongest. Airlines and cruise operators gained on lower expected fuel costs.

Oil fell on potential progress in US-Iran diplomacy. Brent dropped about 5.5% to USD 93 a barrel and WTI fell toward USD 87. Lower energy costs eased near-term inflation concerns ahead of Tuesday's US CPI report.

UBS reads Monday's rebound as dip buying and a reversal of some of last week's sharp derisking. The chip and AI infrastructure decline was amplified by elevated positioning, high expectations and uncertainty over data center development. UBS calls the sell-off a positioning reset, not the start of a lasting downturn in the AI investment cycle.

Breadth supports this view. Last week's weakness was concentrated in chips, data center companies and highly valued growth stocks, while Monday's gains spread across most sectors. UBS reads this as investors differentiating between companies and parts of the AI ecosystem rather than reassessing the growth and earnings outlook.

AI demand remains strong per UBS: recent earnings show accelerating cloud revenue and growing advance orders for computing capacity. UBS forecasts aggregate AI capital spending of USD 1.0tr in 2026, USD 1.4tr in 2027 and USD 1.5tr in 2028. Political and physical constraints may delay, relocate or raise the cost of data center projects but are unlikely to eliminate demand.

Risks remain. Investors increasingly want evidence that AI spending will produce sustainable revenue, utilization and returns. High expectations and concentrated positioning make single companies sensitive to guidance, regulation, financing conditions and sentiment. UBS says further tech volatility would not be surprising.

The oil market stays vulnerable after earlier supply disruption and inventory drawdowns. Diplomatic progress could push prices lower, while renewed attacks or a breakdown in talks could quickly reverse the move.

Tuesday's CPI report is the next test. Strong October employment data have kept expectations for a December Fed rate increase alive. A hotter reading could lift bond yields and challenge the equity rebound, while contained price pressure would support a measured tightening cycle.

UBS sees potential gains in broad equity indices over the next 6-12 months. Its three portfolio suggestions: manage concentration risk (keep AI exposure but trim oversized single-tech positions into strength, favor established platforms with existing compute capacity, visible AI revenue, strong balance sheets and internal funding), rebalance across sectors and regions (preferred US sectors industrials and health care, Eurozone preferred with similar 2027 earnings growth to the US but lower valuations), and build a multi-asset core (rebuild bond allocations in high quality short- and medium-term bonds, with alternatives and broad commodities as hedges against geopolitical or inflation shocks).

tension_points.bear_case: Investors want evidence that AI spending produces sustainable revenue, utilization and returns. Positioning is concentrated, expectations are high, and guidance, regulation or financing changes could hit single names. UBS says further tech volatility would not be surprising.
